ABSTRACT
The sustainable conversion of biomass wastes into high-performance carbon materials for supercapacitors con -
tinues to present a critical challenge. Herein, a green and facile strategy was proposed to synthesize N/S co-doped 
porous carbons using discarded Osmanthus fragrans flowers as the precursor. By employing a NaCl/ZnCl
2 
molten- 
salt system as a synergistic template/activator and urea as the heteroatom source, hierarchical porous archi -
tectures with interconnected networks were constructed. Systematic investigations revealed that activation 
temperature critically governs pore structure evolution, surface chemistry, and electrochemical performance. 
The optimized O-PC-700 
◦
C sample exhibited a high specific surface area (938.6 m
2 
g
� 1
), a balanced micro-/ 
meso-/macroporosity distribution, and abundant N/S/O functional groups. As a supercapacitor electrode, O-PC- 
700 
◦
C delivered a remarkable specific capacitance of 230 F g
� 1 
at 1 A g
� 1 
in a three-electrode system. The 
symmetric device achieved an exceptional energy density of 68.88 Wh kg
� 1 
at 500 W kg
� 1 
and outstanding 
cycling stability (retaining almost 100 % capacitance after 10,000 cycles). The dual activation mechanism of 
molten salts and heteroatom doping synergistically enhances ion accessibility, pseudo-capacitance, and con -
ductivity. This work not only advances the sustainable valorization of floral biomass but also provides a versatile 
strategy for designing hierarchical carbon materials for high-energy-density energy storage systems.
1. Introduction
The escalating global energy crisis, resulting from excessive fossil 
fuel consumption and accompanying CO
2 
emissions, has intensified the 
demand for sustainable energy solutions and advanced energy storage 
technologies [1] . Among emerging energy storage systems, super -
capacitors (SCs, also known as electrochemical capacitors) have 
garnered significant scientific attention as hybrid devices bridging the 
performance gap between conventional dielectric capacitors and 
rechargeable batteries [2,3] . These devices feature three distinct ad -
vantages over conventional energy storage systems: exceptional char -
ge/discharge kinetics that enable rapid energy delivery within seconds, 
unparalleled cycle stability exceeding 100,000 cycles with minimal 
capacitance decay, and superior power density (typically 10 – 100 times 
higher than lithium-ion batteries) [4,5] . Particularly, electrical 
double-layer capacitors (EDLCs), which rely on physical charge 
adsorption/desorption at electrode-electrolyte interfaces, demonstrate 
remarkable rate capability and cycling performance compared to pseu -
docapacitive systems [2,6] .
Carbon-based materials, including activated carbon, carbon nano -
tubes, graphene, and carbon fibers, are predominantly employed in the 
design of supercapacitor electrodes due to their tunable physicochem -
ical properties and robust electrochemical stability [7,8] . The perfor -
mance of these materials is principally governed by three critical 
parameters: (i) heteroatom doping configurations, (ii) accessible specific 
surface area (S
BET
), and (iii) hierarchical pore architecture [9,10 ] . 
Strategic incorporation of nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, or sulfur het -
eroatoms into carbon matrices induces electron density redistribution, 
which simultaneously enhances electrical conductivity through 
defect-induced charge carrier mobility and introduces

pseudo-capacitance via Faradaic redox reactions [11,12] . While high 
S
BET 
theoretically maximizes electric double-layer capacitance by 
providing abundant charge adsorption sites, practical capacitance often 
deviates from ideal predictions due to ineffective pore utilization. This 
discrepancy highlights the essential role of multimodal pore systems: 
micropores ( < 2 nm) dominate ion adsorption capacity via size-selective 
charge accumulation, mesopores (2 – 50 nm) facilitate rapid ion trans -
port kinetics by reducing Warburg impedance, and macropores 
( > 50 nm) act as ion reservoirs to alleviate concentration polarization 
under high current densities [13] . Such hierarchical architectures 
enable synergistic optimization of energy density and power density, 
integrating kinetic efficiency with storage capacity.
Although activated carbons remain industrial benchmarks due to 
their exceptional S
BET 
(~3000 m
2 
g
� 1
) and cost-effectiveness, their 
reliance on non-renewable precursors (e.g., petroleum pitch) raises 
sustainability concerns [14,15] . Biomass-derived carbon materials have 
emerged as sustainable alternatives to conventional carbon precursors, 
offering three key advantages: (i) cost-effectiveness derived from 
abundant renewable sources, (ii) intrinsic heteroatom self-doping (N, O, 
P), and (iii) naturally hierarchical pore structures [16 – 18] . The inherent 
heteroatomic configurations (typically 2 – 8 at% nitrogen content) 
significantly enhance electrode-electrolyte wettability and facilitate 
charge transfer kinetics via induced dipole interactions, as demonstrated 
in various plant-derived systems, such as longan shells [19] , peach gum 
[20] , ginkgo leaves [21] , peanut shell [22] , Sargassum natans [23] , 
mangosteen shells [24] , and many other materials. Osmanthus fragrans , a 
lignocellulosic ornamental species within the Oleaceae family, shows 
promise for sustainable carbon engineering. With global annual flower 
production exceeding 500,000 metric tons, approximately 70 % of 
post-harvest biomass is currently discarded as agricultural waste. This 
underutilized resource contains unique biochemical 
components-including 18 – 22 wt% lignin and 12 – 15 wt% 
flavonoids-that enable dual functionality during pyrolysis: serving as 
natural pore-forming agents while simultaneously generating 
nitrogen-oxygen co-doped active sites.
Eutectic salts, composed of two or more inorganic salts with a 
melting point substantially lower than that of their individual compo -
nents, have recently emerged as promising activating agents for the 
synthesis of carbon-based materials [25 – 27] . This unique class of molten 
salt mixtures offers distinct advantages over conventional chemical ac -
tivators (e.g., KOH or ZnCl
2
) in terms of tunable composition, 
cost-effectiveness, and reduced environmental impact. The ionic nature 
of eutectic salts enables efficient mass transport during 
high-temperature activation processes, facilitating the creation of hier -
archically porous carbon architectures with ultrahigh specific surface 
areas and tailored pore size distributions. Notably, the synergistic effects 
among mixed salt ions (e.g., chloride, carbonate, or nitrate species) 
promote the simultaneous carbonization and activation, thereby 
yielding defect-rich graphitic domains that enhance electrical conduc -
tivity while maintaining structural stability. For instance, Liu et al. Liu 
et al. utilized a one-pot molten salt (KCl/KHCO
3
) pyrolysis method, 
employing a mixture of coal tar pitch and agar to synthesize mesoporous 
carbon [28] . This approach yielded a material with small pores and a 
bimodal pore size distribution, where the infiltration of the molten salt 
throughout the carbon precursor enabled homogeneous activation, 
facilitating the formation of this bimodal structure. Consequently, the 
resulting carbon possessed a three-dimensionally interconnected hier -
archical architecture, exhibiting an ultrahigh specific surface area of 
1965 m
2 
g
� 1 
and a well-balanced pore size distribution. Another 
instance, Jia et al., fabricated nitrogen and sulfur co-doped graphene- -
like carbon nanosheets with a hierarchical pore structure using a molten 
salt activation method [29] . The as-prepared carbon nanosheets 
exhibited a large specific surface area of 1753.01 m
2 
g
� 1 
and a hierar -
chical pore structure. Moreover, the electrode made from these carbon 
nanosheets demonstrated a high specific capacitance of 262.4 F g
� 1 
at a 
current density of 1 A g
� 1
.
Herein, we reported a sustainable strategy to fabricate N/S co-doped 
hierarchical porous carbon from discarded Osmanthus fragrans flowers 
via NaCl/ZnCl
2 
eutectic salt activation and urea-assisted heteroatom 
doping. Systematic investigation revealed that 700 
◦
C-optimized 
carbonization yielded interconnected pore networks (938.6 m
2 
g
� 1
) 
with balanced micro/meso/macroporosity, while the dual heteroatoms 
significantly enhance surface electrochemical reactivity and electrical 
conductivity. The resultant O-PC-700 
◦
C exhibited superior capacitance 
(230 F g
� 1 
at 1 A g
� 1
) and exceptional energy density (68.88 Wh kg
� 1
) 
in symmetric supercapacitors, paired with ultrastable cycling perfor -
mance (nearly 100 % capacitance retention after 10,000 cycles). This 
study highlights the synergistic effect between molten-salt templating 
and heteroatom engineering for developing biomass-derived high-per -
formance energy storage materials.
2. Experimental sections
2.1. Materials
Fresh Osmanthus fragrans flowers were collected from trees on the 
campus of Suzhou University. Urea (CH
4
N
2
O), Zinc chloride (ZnCl
2
), 
Sodium chloride (NaCl), polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE, 60 wt% sus -
pension), hydrochloric acid and ethanol were purchased from Aladdin 
Chemistry (China) Co., Ltd. All chemicals in this study were in analytical 
reagent grade without any further treatment. Deionized (DI) water was 
utilized throughout the experimental procedures for all treatment 
processes.
2.2. Synthesis of PC from Osmanthus fragrans
The Osmanthus fragrans -derived carbon materials were synthesized 
via a controlled thermal activation protocol as depicted in Fig. 1 . Fresh 
Osmanthus fragrans flowers were first rinsed with deionized water to 
remove surface impurities, followed by dehydration in a vacuum oven at 
105 
◦
C for 24 h. The dried biomass was then homogenously mixed with 
the dual-activator system (ZnCl
2
: NaCl = 2:1, w/w) at an optimized 
precursor-to-activator mass ratio of 3:1. The mixture was magnetically 
stirred in DI water at room temperature for 24 h to ensure thorough ionic 
infiltration, followed by vacuum drying at 105 
◦
C until a constant weight 
was attained.
The subsequent thermal treatment was conducted in a horizontal 
tube furnace under continuous N
2 
flow. After 30 min of purging to 
establish an oxygen-free environment, the temperature was pro -
grammed to rise at 5 
◦
C min
� 1 
to target temperatures (600 – 900 
◦
C) with 
a 2 h isothermal holding period. The cooled products were sequentially 
washed with 1 M hydrochloric acid solution and DI water until reaching 
a neutral pH, involving intermediate centrifugation steps to remove 
soluble residues. Final drying at 105 
◦
C for 12 h yielded activated carbon 
materials designated as O-PC-T, where T represents pyrolysis tempera -
ture (600 – 900 
◦
C). A control sample (O-PC) was prepared under iden -
tical conditions without activating agents, with the pyrolysis 
temperature set at 700 
◦
C to match the optimized O-PC-700 
◦
C sample.
2.3. Fabrication of supercapacitors
The working electrodes were fabricated through a standardized 
slurry-coating protocol optimized for carbon-based supercapacitors. 
First, the active material (as-prepared carbon), conductive agent (acet -
ylene black), and binder (PTFE) were homogenously blended in ethanol 
solution at a mass ratio of 16:3:1. This mixture was then precisely coated 
onto pre-cleaned nickel foam substrates (1 × 1.5 cm
2
) using a doctor 
blade apparatus. Finally, the electrodes were dried at 80 
◦
C for 12 h to 
remove residual solvent. The resulting active mass loading of 2.5 
± 0.2 mg cm
� 2 
was carefully controlled within the optimal range 
(2 – 3 mg cm
� 2
) for balancing capacitive performance and charge trans -
fer kinetics, as recommended in supercapacitor standardization studies.
